ety.text: From Middle English cage, from Old French cage, from Latin cavea. Doublet of cadge and cavea and related to jail.

senses.d: An enclosure made of spaced bars, normally to hold animals while providing some ventilation.
ex: We keep a bird in a cage.
The tigers are in a cage to protect the public.

senses.d: The passenger compartment of a lift.

ex: My body is a cage / That keeps me from dancing with the one I love / But my mind holds the key

senses.d: The area from which competitors throw a discus or hammer.
An outer framework of timber, enclosing something within it.
A skeleton frame to limit the motion of a loose piece, such as a ball valve.
A wirework strainer, used in connection with pumps and pipes.
To confine in a cage; to put into and keep in a cage.
ex: And the row of human captors, ever leering, They who caged me, Know their power and gloat on my captivity.
The industrial practice of caging commercial laying hens has given caged housing a bad narne.
The serial killer was caged for life.

senses.d: To restrict someone's movement or creativity.

ex: To prevent damage to its gimbal mountings during extreme aerobatic maneuvers, the navball should be caged before the start of a display sequence.

senses.d: To track individual responses to direct mail, either (advertising) to maintain and develop mailing lists or (politics) to identify people who are not eligible to vote because they do not reside at the registered addresses.

ety.text: Inherited from Old French cage, from Latin cavea. This form did not undergo the palatalization of c before a.
From Latin cavea. Doublet of cavea, a later borrowing. Cognates include Catalan gàbia, English cage, Sicilian jaggia

Old French jaiolebor. Old Spanish ja(v)ola Spanish jaula Inherited from Old Spanish ja(v)ola, borrowed from Old French jaiole, from Late Latin caveola, from Latin cavea (“cage”) + -ola (diminutive ending). Doublet of gayola, which was inherited. Cognates include English jail.

Likely from Aragonese gayola, from Late Latin caveola, diminutive from Latin cavea (“cage”) (whence Old Spanish gabia, gavia). Compare Portuguese gaiola. Doublet of jaula, which was borrowed through French.
From Old Galician-Portuguese, from Late Latin caveola, diminutive from Latin cavea. Cognate to Spanish gayola. Compare jaula, a doublet borrowed through French.

Old French jaiolebor. Portuguese jaula Borrowed from Old French jaiole, from Late Latin caveola, from Latin cavea (“cage”) + -ola (diminutive ending). Compare gaiola, an inherited doublet, and Spanish jaula, likewise borrowed from French.

es:cabina.gl: cabin (the passenger area of an airplane)

ety.text: English cabinbor. French cabinebor. Spanish cabina Borrowed from French cabine.

pt:engaiolar.gl: to cage (to put into a cage)
